description: We are a multidisciplinary team of innovators, developers, and researchers passionate about space technology, artificial intelligence, and Earth observation. We aim to transform NASA's open data into meaningful solutions using machine learning, satellite imagery, and creative problem-solving. United by curiosity and collaboration, we strive to develop innovative technologies that address real-world challenges and make a positive impact on our planet.
summary:
SarezWatch watches the slopes above Lake Sarez in Tajikistan, a lake held back
by the tallest dam on Earth — one no engineer ever built. A 1911 earthquake
dropped a mountainside into the Murghab valley, trapping 17 km³ of water. An
estimated five million people live along the rivers below, in four countries.
The danger is not the dam but the slopes above it: a landslide into the lake
raises a wave that could overtop it. No one can watch those slopes from the
ground: 3,000–6,000 m, days from any road, snowbound half the year. Satellites
can. SarezWatch runs two radars through one pipeline and compares them pixel
for pixel: NASA's NISAR, L-band, June–October 2026, and ESA's Sentinel-1,
C-band, 2020–2025. L-band returns measurements on 67.6% of this terrain where
C-band returns 43.2%; the five-year C-band stack carries the time depth that
millimetres a year demand. From that stack SarezWatch maps how every
300-metre patch of ground moved, then lets an unsupervised model flag what
moves unlike anywhere else, blind to the dam's location. It found a slope
3.8 km above the dam sliding 65 mm a year, debated since 2000, and the dam
itself stable.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SarezWatch answers one question: which slopes around Lake Sarez are moving, and how fast. It is a web application built around a map. Every coloured dot is a patch of ground roughly 300 by 300 metres with a measured displacement history. Click one and you see its graph: how that ground moved from pass to pass between January 2020 and January 2025, with the large earthquakes that fall inside the window marked on it. A second panel holds the same valley as NASA's NISAR sees it, so the two radars can be read side by side.

On top of the measurement, an algorithm finds the patches behaving unlike the rest of the valley and explains each find in words: where it is, how fast it moves, how trustworthy the measurement is, and what the score does not mean. The valley is a first target, not a special case: the same pipeline runs anywhere NISAR and Sentinel-1 fly, and the study area is built from map geometry rather than hard-coded.

HOW IT WORKS

SarezWatch runs on two radars: NASA's NISAR, flying L-band at a wavelength of 24 cm, and ESA's Sentinel-1, flying C-band at 5.5 cm. A satellite sends a radio wave at the ground and catches the reflection. If the ground has shifted between two passes, the wave comes back on a different phase, and that shift is the measurement. Wavelengths of a few centimetres are what make millimetres measurable from 700 kilometres up.

The two radars are good at different things, and the application uses both. The longer L-band wave keeps its coherence on rough, snow-touched slopes where the shorter C-band wave loses it, so NISAR returns usable measurements on 67.6 % of this terrain against 43.2 % for Sentinel-1. Sentinel-1, in orbit since 2014, brings the one thing NISAR cannot yet: five years of passes, which is what millimetres a year are measured out of.

Both go through the same pipeline, in five steps.

First, the study area is derived from the map rather than drawn by hand. The outlines of the lake and the blockage come from OpenStreetMap, are merged, buffered by 10 km, and the same geometry yields four analysis zones.

Second, interferograms are retrieved for both radars: Sentinel-1 products published by the UK COMET LiCSAR facility, and NISAR L2 GUNW products from the ASF DAAC. Only the window covering our area is read from each product, using HTTP range requests, so a 37 MB product costs about 5 MB. In total, 358 Sentinel-1 pairs across 146 acquisition dates, and 8 NISAR pairs across 9 dates between 25 June and 11 October 2026.

Third, the pairs become a time series. Each interferogram has its ramp and its elevation-correlated term removed, everything is tied to a single reference window chosen automatically as the most consistently stable patch, the network is screened by phase-triplet loop closure, and a small-baseline inversion yields cumulative displacement and velocity for every pixel. The NISAR chain is handled on its own terms: its ionospheric phase screen is subtracted first, because an L-band wave is delayed by the ionosphere almost twenty times more than a C-band one, and its daisy-chain network is summed rather than inverted.

Fourth, each measured patch is described by features of motion: velocity, acceleration, scatter, seasonal amplitude, cumulative displacement.

Fifth, an Isolation Forest ML model ranks patches by how unusual their behaviour is, a Local Outlier Factor and a robust z-score check the result independently, and DBSCAN gathers isolated flags into spatial clusters.

WHAT BENEFITS IT HAS

Below Lake Sarez, along the Bartang, Panj and Amu Darya rivers, an estimated five million people live across four countries. The danger is not that the blockage will wash away; it has held for a century. The danger is the slopes around it: a large landslide falling into the lake would raise a wave capable of overtopping it.

Those slopes cannot be watched from the ground. They stand between 3,000 and 6,000 metres, days from the nearest road, under snow half the year, and in 2015 a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck directly beneath the lake. None of that troubles a satellite.

The system found a patch 3.8 km upstream of the dam moving at 65 millimetres a year, which has accumulated a third of a metre of displacement over five years. It is the Right Bank Landslide, the feature specialists have debated since 2000. The algorithm was never told where to look. And separately: the blockage itself came back stable, zero flags, under a millimetre a year.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

That the decision about which slope to look at first is made from a measurement rather than from intuition. The system does not predict landslides and does not replace a specialist. It sorts the terrain by how unusual each place is and says where attention, and a field visit, is worth spending.

Nothing in the processing is tuned to Sarez. The study area is built from OpenStreetMap geometry, the radar products come from open archives, and the detector is given no knowledge of this valley, so the same pipeline runs on any landslide-dammed lake in the Alpine-Himalayan belt — and there are hundreds of them above inhabited valleys.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Processing: Python 3.12, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely, rasterio, h5py, scikit-learn.

Backend: FastAPI, across 19 endpoints.

Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Plotly.

Infrastructure: Docker Compose, nginx, Netlify.

Quality: pytest, 64 tests.

Data: Sentinel-1 through COMET LiCSAR (CEDA and JASMIN), NISAR L2 GUNW through the ASF DAAC, product discovery through NASA CMR and ASF Search, terrain from Copernicus DEM GLO-30 on AWS Open Data, earthquakes from the USGS FDSN event service, and geometry from OpenStreetMap via Overpass. NISAR data courtesy of NASA/ISRO. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel-1 data, 2020-2025. Map geometry (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL.

AI assistance: the code and the documentation were written with an AI coding assistant. Every number in SarezWatch comes from the pipeline running over the data listed above - no measurement, figure or map here is AI-generated, and the application contains no synthetic deformation data.

HOW THE PROJECT IS CREATIVE

The central decision is that the detector is deliberately blinded. It never sees coherence, uncertainty, elevation, slope or distance to the dam. A model given data quality quickly learns to flag noisy pixels, and a noisy pixel is not a moving one. A model given distance to the dam starts taking an interest in the dam's surroundings, and the find stops proving anything. That constraint is exactly what makes the right-bank result convincing.

Second, every flag explains itself in words. The system does not hand over a bare number: it names which features made the patch unusual, which way the surface moved relative to the satellite, how much downslope motion the radar can see on a slope that steep, and how far the measurement itself can be trusted. The text is generated, not written by hand, and it accompanies every find.

Third, a negative result is published alongside a positive one. The challenge asks for a hypothesis about what you see in SAR data, or do not see. Most systems show only what they found. We also show what the newer radar cannot see yet, explain precisely why, and say when that will change.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Where there is no measurement, we draw nothing. The radar returns no usable signal from 57 % of this terrain: shadow, layover, decorrelated snow. Those pixels are absent from the data, left blank on the map, and flagged in the API. Painting them green would be the easiest lie in this field.

Displacement is measured along the radar line of sight and is never called vertical or horizontal. The anomaly score is a rank of unusualness within this dataset, not a probability of failure, and the interface repeats that on every flag.

No labelled inventory of landslides exists for this valley, so the detector has no measured precision or recall. In their place we publish the stability of the result under resampling (0.93), the share of flags that sit inside spatial clusters (85 %), and the agreement between two independent detectors, which is 0.06. That last number is low, and we publish it for exactly that reason.

The NISAR result is negative, and it is reported alongside the others. Across its 108-day archive, the landslide's expected displacement is 20.2 mm while the noise of the measurement is 20.1 mm. The signal-to-noise ratio is 1.01, and the landslide patch is statistically indistinguishable from a random one. This is not a processing failure but a measured limit of a young archive: by our estimate it becomes long enough in about 2.6 years. Even now, L-band already wins on coverage, measuring 67.6 % of the grid against 43.2 % for Sentinel-1.
